summary: An early Telnet option, from 1974, for agreeing how a vertical tab character in output is handled. It follows the same pattern as the related tab and formfeed options from the same author. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: A vertical tab tells a printer to jump down the page. This note lets two computers agree on who handles that jump and how.

subtitle: Deciding who handles vertical tab characters in Telnet output.

tldr.problem: When a vertical tab character is sent over Telnet, the receiving system must decide what to do with it: pass it through, replace it with line-feeds, or discard it. The two sides need to agree on the handling.
tldr.mechanism: The option lets the sender and receiver negotiate via Telnet commands, choosing from eight strategies—ignore the character, simulate it with line-feeds, discard it, delay after it, or wait for a response from the other direction. Values 0 to 255 encode the different strategies.
tldr.outcome: Both sides know how incoming vertical tab characters will be processed. The RFC is Historic and no longer widely used.

today: RFC 657 is Historic and no longer used in practice. Modern terminal applications do not typically support vertical tabs at all, and the negotiation mechanisms defined here are no longer part of standard Telnet implementations.

sections.title: The Telnet Vertical Tab Character Disposition Option
sections.content: RFC 657 defines the NAOVTD option (Negotiate About Output Vertical Tab Disposition), a Telnet option for handling the vertical tab character (ASCII 11) when it appears in output. Like RFC 654 for horizontal tabs, this RFC specifies what happens to a vertical tab character: whether it is sent as-is, replaced with line-feeds, discarded, simulated, or treated some other way. Since different terminals handle vertical tabs differently, negotiation is necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: When a vertical tab character arrives, something has to decide what happens—send it, turn it into line-feeds, skip it, or wait. This option lets two computers agree on that.

sections.title: Vertical Tab Disposition Strategies
sections.content:
The option defines eight strategies, encoded as values 0 to 255. A value of 0 means the sender will handle the vertical tab. Values 1 to 250 mean the receiver should handle it with a delay (the value is the number of NUL characters to insert after the tab). Value 251 means replace the vertical tab with carriage-return/line-feed. Value 252 means discard the vertical tab entirely. Value 253 means simulate the vertical tab by inserting enough line-feeds to reach the next vertical tab stop. Value 254 means wait for a character on the opposite connection before continuing. Value 255 means the receiver should handle it but with no specific instruction.

The governing rule: if both sides want to handle vertical tabs, the sender wins. If neither wants to, the receiver must.
sections.plainLanguage: There are eight choices: I will handle it (0); you handle it with a delay (1-250); replace with line-feeds (251); discard (252); simulate it (253); wait for the other direction (254); or you decide (255).

sections.title: The Negotiation Process
sections.content: The negotiation follows the same protocol as RFC 654. Both sides exchange DO, WILL, DON'T, and WON'T commands to agree on whether to negotiate. Once agreed, they use subnegotiation (IAC SB NAOVTD DS or IAC SB NAOVTD DR) to propose their preferred disposition value. The data sender uses code DS (1) and the receiver uses code DR (0). The RFC notes that delays are implemented by inserting NUL bytes immediately after the vertical tab character, and simulation is done by inserting line-feeds to reach the next stop.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides use standard Telnet negotiation commands, agree on a vertical tab strategy, and then apply it to every vertical tab character until they renegotiate.
